Seven credit card transfer bonuses are active right now, including American Express Membership Rewards to Flying Blue at 25%, expiring October 31, 2026. Here's every active offer, real flights you can book using those programs today, and how to decide whether to move your points. These are transferable points programs — not those with fixed cash-back value — which is what makes the bonus percentage matter so much. This page is continuously updated with current credit card transfer bonuses running across every major program.

What are the current transfer bonuses (October 2026)?

Well, as said above, they can help you save quite a few points, so you can spread your points across more redemptions, splash out with an upgraded seat, or go to a place you might not have been able to afford otherwise. Here are just a few recent examples of great fares found on point.me that are made even better with a credit card transfer bonus.

Active credit card transfer bonuses right now

Each active transfer bonus lets you move transferable points from your credit card issuer's loyalty program into an airline's miles at a better-than-normal rate. The bonus percentage is calculated on the points you transfer — so a 25% bonus on 10,000 points gives you 12,500 miles instead of the standard 10,000, assuming the normal transfer ratio is 1:1. Since transfers are irreversible, it's worth knowing the favorable transfer ratios on offer before you commit.

Why transfer your Amex Membership Rewards points to Hilton Honors right now

The transfer bonus from Amex Membership Rewards to Hilton is worth acting on, but only in specific cases. Typically you'll get more outsized value putting your points toward air, especially premium cabin tickets, and that's usually where your Amex points shine. That said, Amex to Hilton already transfers at a 1-to-2 ratio, and with a 30% bonus on top, 1,000 Amex points becomes 2,600 Hilton Honors points. This won't make you points rich, but it can beat the value you'd get booking hotels through the Amex travel portal. Where it really makes sense is topping off a Hilton balance you're close to redeeming, or setting up a fifth-night-free redemption: as long as you hold Hilton status at Silver or above, you're eligible for the fifth night free on award stays, meaning a five-night booking only costs you four nights in a standard room. Stack the bonus with that benefit and the value gets genuinely compelling. But if you aren't topping off a balance or targeting a fifth-night-free stay, this one isn't worth chasing, and you're better off holding your Amex points for airfare. It's worth noting this is one of the better offers we've seen in years from Amex to Hilton Honors, so while it's one of the better offers to come around, it still isn't a redeem-in-all-cases proposition.

Why transfer your Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Marriott Bonvoy right now

The transfer bonus from Chase Ultimate Rewards to Marriott Bonvoy looks tempting on paper, but for most people it's still not worth acting on. A Bonvoy point is worth far less than a Chase point, and even with the bonus, the math doesn't come close to what your Ultimate Rewards can get you through Points Boost on select travel, let alone by transferring to one of Chase's higher-value airline or hotel partners. The exception is if you're already planning a stay with your existing Bonvoy points and need a few more, whether that's to take advantage of the fifth night free on award stays or to top off a free night certificate. In those cases, it can make sense, especially if you have a large Chase balance. Otherwise, it may be cheaper to buy Marriott points directly during one of their purchase promotions and save your Chase points for a better redemption down the road.

Why transfer your Citi ThankYou points to avianca lifemiles right now

The transfer bonus from Citi ThankYou to avianca lifemiles is worth acting on if Citi ThankYou is the only transferable currency you have and you're booking a last-minute award ticket on avianca or a Star Alliance partner. lifemiles uses fixed redemption rates on partner-operated flights, which can deliver some of the lowest pricing out there compared to what other programs charge. That said, avianca is a transfer partner of many other transferable currencies, so if you have other options, you're probably better off earmarking your Citi ThankYou points for a exclusive transfer partner such as Japan Airlines Mileage Bank or EVA Air Infinity MileageLands. One caveat: lifemiles customer service is weak, cancellation fees are high, and reticketing after a schedule change can be a headache, so this is a buyer-beware program best reserved for travel within a few weeks rather than further out.

Why transfer your Citi ThankYou points to Japan Airlines Mileage Bank right now

The transfer bonus from Citi ThankYou to Japan Airlines (JAL) Mileage Bank is worth acting on, especially if you're looking to travel to Japan, as they release far more availability to members of their own program versus partner programs. JAL also has fantastic pricing on partner flights, including British Airways, Emirates, and many others, so even if you aren't flying to Japan on JAL metal, routing a partner redemption through JAL can deliver strong rates and, in some cases, lower taxes and fees than booking direct or through another partner program, British Airways being a prime example. It is worth noting the downsides, though: JAL Mileage Bank has a strict 36-month mileage expiry that cannot be extended, so this isn't a program to speculatively move points into if you're not ready to redeem. There are also restrictions on who you can redeem for, with award tickets limited to the member themselves and their family.

Why transfer your Amex Membership Rewards points to Aeromexico Rewards right now

The transfer bonus from Amex Membership Rewards to Aeromexico Rewards is worth acting on if you're flying to or within Mexico, especially when cash fares are high, since Aeromexico releases more award availability on its own flights than it does to partner programs. It can also be a strong option for South America if connecting through Mexico City isn't much of a detour, which tends to be the case for travelers west of the Mississippi. Even Texans headed to Europe may find good value, though Aeromexico's European route network is limited compared to other major airlines. The big catch is the booking experience: the website defaults to Spanish even when set to English, so you'll likely need translation tools, the app, or a call to a customer service line that isn't particularly helpful either.

Why transfer your Amex Membership Rewards points to Flying Blue right now

The transfer bonus from Amex Membership Rewards to Flying Blue is worth acting on if you're booking a flight to Europe, or beyond it to Africa, the Middle East, or Asia. Flying Blue's dynamic pricing keeps steady availability on its own Air France and KLM flights, and rates on partners like Virgin Atlantic and China. One nice perk for families: children aged 2 to 11 traveling with an adult get a 25% discount on award tickets, which adds up on a trip you'd otherwise pay full price for.

Why transfer your Capital One Miles to The British Airways Club right now

The transfer bonus from Capital One Miles to The British Airways Club is worth acting on, especially since we haven't seen one in close to a year. The British Airways Club has some of the best availability on its own flights to Europe from North America, as they release more award availability to members of their own program versus partner programs. The taxes and fees run high, but if there's a British Airways flight from your home airport, it can be worth paying for the convenience versus connecting via another city. What's also unique to the Avios currency itself: if your account qualifies, you can move Avios between programs like Aer Lingus AerClub, Iberia Club, Finnair Plus, and Qatar Airways Privilege Club, a flexibility that no other loyalty currency offers.

Should you transfer? What to think through before you move points.

Transfers are irreversible. Once your Amex or Chase points move to an airline program, they don’t come back. That’s not a reason to avoid transferring — it’s a reason to be deliberate.

Transfer now if: You’ve found a specific flight on point.me, confirmed the award availability is live with the airline or loyalty program, and a transfer bonus is active for that program. That’s the ideal scenario. Do it.

Wait if: You don’t have a specific flight in mind. Holding transferable points in your credit card account keeps your options open across all transfer partners — airline and hotel partners alike.

One exception: If you frequently book with a specific airline program and feel confident you’ll use the miles within the next few weeks, an active transfer bonus of 25% or more may be worth acting on without a confirmed booking. Outside of that scenario, avoid speculative transfers — keep your points flexible until you’re ready to book a specific redemption.

Why speculative transfers almost always backfire

The value of a transferable currency is optionality. The moment you transfer, you surrender three forms of protection — and most travelers don’t think carefully about all three before hitting the button.

Expiration risk. Card programs don’t expire your points as long as your account is open. Many airline programs do, particularly those outside the United States. Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer miles expire on a hard three-year clock regardless of activity. Emirates Skywards miles expire on a similar hard schedule. No amount of partner activity, paid-flight credit, or additional transfers extends the clock once it starts. If life intervenes and your trip gets pushed or cancelled, those miles may quietly run out.

Devaluation risk. Airline programs change their award charts — sometimes overnight, often without notice. 100,000 miles that would have covered two business-class seats to Europe before a devaluation may only cover one after. A balance held in Amex Membership Rewards, Chase Ultimate Rewards, or Capital One Miles is insulated from any single program’s changes. Miles sitting in an airline account are not.

Availability risk. You can only redeem miles if award space exists on the route and dates you want. Some programs cap award inventory tightly; others use dynamic pricing, where inventory is technically always there but at prices that can spike to 500,000+ miles per ticket in worst cases. You can’t know today whether the exact seat you want will exist when you’re ready to book.

When does a speculative transfer actually make sense?

Two narrow cases. First, if you frequently redeem through a specific program — Air Canada Aeroplan, Flying Blue, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club — and a bonus to that program is running, topping up during the bonus usually pays for itself inside a year. Second, if you’re points-rich across multiple issuers (high six figures of transferable currency) and can afford to lock some capital into a specific program as a hedge. Most readers don’t sit in either category. For everyone else, wait until you’ve confirmed the seat.

point.me take

A 30% transfer bonus to a program you don’t understand is a worse deal than a 0% bonus to one you do. The bonus percentage is tempting, like any discount. The program is what actually matters. We see it constantly — people rush to transfer 50,000 Chase points to Virgin Atlantic because the bonus looks great, then realize they have no idea how to find Delta One availability or what a good redemption rate looks like. The bonus amplifies a good decision. It doesn’t rescue a bad one. Before you move a single point, search point.me and confirm the flight you want actually exists at the price you expect. If it does, a transfer bonus is a genuine gift. If it doesn’t, no percentage will save you.

— Jimmy Yoon, Head of Points Intelligence · point.me

Which programs offer the most active credit card transfer bonuses?

Not all major programs run transfer bonus offers at the same frequency. Based on the full dataset, American Express Membership Rewards and Citi ThankYou Rewards run transfer bonus offers more than any other bank point programs — with avianca lifemiles alone receiving nearly a dozen Amex bonuses over the tracked period. Chase Ultimate Rewards follows closely behind, while Capital One Miles runs offers less frequently but has shown up for key programs like JAL Mileage Bank and Virgin Atlantic. If catching current credit card transfer bonuses regularly is a goal, an Amex or Citi card gives you significantly better odds.

Flying Blue (Air France/KLM) receives credit card transfer bonuses from more programs more frequently than any other airline — bonused by Amex, Chase, Citi, Capital One, Bilt, and even Choice Rewards, making it the most universally supported destination in the dataset. Other programs worth watching include avianca lifemiles, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, and British Airways Club, all of which see consistent activity across multiple sources. Less frequent but high-value programs — JAL Mileage Bank, Etihad Guest, Qatar Airways Privilege Club — tend to run strong offers when they do appear.

25% is among the most common transfer bonus amounts at the high end for traditional card programs, with 20% and 30% the most frequently recurring figures overall. A 30%+ offer is genuinely above average. Historically, bonuses from traditional card programs can reach 40–50%, with Citi ThankYou hitting 50% to Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles and Amex reaching 40% to both Virgin Atlantic and British Airways. Bilt operates differently — occasionally running 100–150% credit card transfer bonuses for a single day on Rent Day, which are extraordinary by any measure but require fast action given their extremely short windows. New transfer bonus offers typically drop at the start of the calendar month and are usually publicly announced by each credit card issuer.

What is each frequently bonused program actually good for?

The bonus list itself doesn’t answer the real question: which of these programs should you actually use? A 30% bonus to a program you don’t know how to redeem is just a discount on a currency you have no plan to spend. Here’s the one-liner on each of the airline programs that get bonused most often — from Jimmy Yoon, point.me’s Head of Points Intelligence.

Air Canada Aeroplan

One of the best all-around airline programs, period. Aeroplan’s value comes from two places: an enormous partner roster that includes unique non-Star Alliance partners like Emirates and Oman Air, and competitively low cash co-pays — Aeroplan doesn’t charge fuel surcharges on its own members’ redemptions. Particularly strong for long-haul business class between the U.S. and Europe, and one of the only practical ways to book long-haul Singapore Airlines awards, which KrisFlyer rarely releases to other partners. If you fly multiple times a year and Aeroplan is one of your regular programs, a bonus here is close to a no-brainer.

Flying Blue (Air France KLM)

The program we recommend most often when it gets bonused. Flying Blue uses dynamic pricing with a wide range — sometimes awards are as low as 50,000 miles in business class to Europe; sometimes they’re 500,000 — but when prices are reasonable, they’re very reasonable. Two use cases stand out: Virgin Atlantic award flights booked through Flying Blue often come with several hundred dollars lower taxes and fees per passenger than booking through Virgin directly, and Flying Blue offers genuinely competitive rates on domestic Delta flights inside the U.S.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club

Valuable for both own-metal and partner redemptions. Flying Club miles offer solid pricing on Virgin Atlantic's own Upper Class — dynamic pricing means transatlantic business class can be had for around 35,000 points, though taxes and fees run high. A strong choice if London is your destination or a convenient stopover. On the partner side, Air France and KLM Economy flights are the standout redemptions. Availability is quite good for most of the year, even during peak travel months. 

The Avios Family (British Airways, Iberia Club, Qatar Privilege Club, Aer Lingus AerClub, and Finnair Plus)

These four programs all use the Avios currency and allow you to freely move points between them — subject to name-matching and account-seasoning rules (accounts generally need to be 30–60 days old with matching contact details). That cross-program flexibility is unique in the loyalty space and changes the math on every Avios bonus: a bonus into any one of the four effectively gives you access to all four. Qatar Privilege Club offers more Qsuite business-class availability to its own members than to partner programs — so it’s the best way to book Qatar’s award-winning business product. British Airways Executive Club opens up more availability on BA metal, which matters if you live near a London-served U.S. hub. Iberia Club and Aer Lingus AerClub are strongest for transatlantic Europe redemptions from specific gateway cities.

avianca lifemiles

lifeMiles is a Star Alliance program with low taxes and fees on partner redemptions — similar to Aeroplan on that front. But because avianca regularly runs its own mileage sales where you can buy lifemiles at roughly the same effective rate a good transfer bonus achieves, we rarely recommend transferring unless your balance is genuinely flush. The trade-off: avianca’s customer service and cancellation policies are less forgiving than peer programs, which matters more in today’s environment of frequent schedule changes and cancellations.

Japan Airlines Mileage Bank, Aer Lingus AerClub, Qantas Frequent Flyer

Three programs that don’t bonus often but reward paying attention when they do. JAL Mileage Bank offers one of the best distance-based award charts for oneworld redemptions and one of the best ways of booking flights to/from Japan, as they release more availability to their own members. Aer Lingus AerClub offers a competitive award chart to Europe from the East Coast with low taxes, so it’s a great way to book travel to Europe if you’re price conscious. Qantas Frequent Flyer is one of the better ways to book oneworld partner awards, particularly on domestic US flights, when a connection is required between your origin and destination.

Do annual fees affect transfer bonus value?

Most cards with the richest transfer partners — and most frequent access to transfer bonus offers — carry annual fees. The Chase Sapphire Reserve runs $795/year. The Amex Platinum is $895/year. Chase Sapphire Preferred is $95/year and Citi Strata Premier is $95/year and still provides full access to transfer partners and any current credit card transfer active bonuses.

A single well-timed transfer bonus can meaningfully offset an annual fee. Transfer bonuses are one of the most concrete ways to measure whether a premium travel card is paying for itself — more so than points earned on eligible purchases or credits for streaming services, car rentals, or online groceries. For travelers newer to award travel, starting with a lower annual fee card and building toward a premium card as you get comfortable with the transfer process is often the right sequence.

Hotel programs and transfer bonuses

Most transfer bonus activity involves airline programs, but hotel programs occasionally appear as transfer partners. Marriott Bonvoy points, Hilton Honors, Wyndham Rewards, and programs affiliated with Leading Hotels of the World and Preferred Hotels appear as transfer options from some card issuers. However, hotel transfer ratios are generally less favorable than airline transfer ratios, and hotel-focused credit card transfer bonuses are rare. If you’re optimizing for flight redemptions — which is where the good value in award travel consistently lives — airline programs are where the meaningful bonus activity happens.

There is one narrow exception worth knowing about. American Express Membership Rewards to Hilton Honors already transfers at a 1:2 ratio, and when Amex runs a bonus on this transfer (historically up to 25%), the effective ratio gets high enough to make sense if you’re booking a specific Hilton stay you’re already committed to — particularly at aspirational properties like Conrad Maldives or Waldorf Astoria Los Cabos. Even then, an airline transfer will usually return more value per Amex point. The other case where a hotel transfer bonus can make sense: topping off a Hilton or Marriott account by a small amount to complete a specific booking, where the alternative is buying points outright at a worse effective rate.

If you’re not booking a specific stay or topping off for a specific redemption, a hotel transfer bonus is almost always a distraction. Keep the points flexible.

When do transfer bonuses typically drop?

Current credit card transfer bonus offers typically drop at the start of the calendar month. Mid-month launches happen, but they're less common — so the first few business days of each month are when it pays to check most closely. Bilt Rewards is the exception: Bilt's one-time bonus drops are announced for the first of every month.

Seasonality beyond the monthly cadence is less pronounced. September and October do show more activity in the historical data, but there's no consistent "fall surge" across issuers — the elevated count reflects a handful of programs running overlapping promotions, not a tide that lifts all boats. The most-bonused airline partners (Flying Blue, Virgin Atlantic, avianca lifemiles) keep relatively steady pacing across seasons, with offers appearing in nearly every quarter. The practical takeaway: don't hold out for a "better season" to catch a bonus you need. If an offer fits your redemption plan, act on it.
